cultivar: Korean red pine or Manchurian red pine; Korean pine for jannip-cha
processing: Needles are soaked, rinsed, trimmed of their sharp tips and cut, then used fresh or shade-dried and infused over low heat. A second style ferments the needles in sugar water for a week or more.
harvest_season: Usually around December, preferably before midday, from 10- to 20-year-old trees in sunny mid-mountain spots.
appearance_dry: Short cut lengths of needle, a dull dark green when dried.
appearance_liquor: Typically pale yellow-green and clear; the fermented style is filtered through cloth.
appearance_wet: Soft green needle pieces, normally strained off before drinking.
taste_profile: Astringent enough that honey or sugar is the usual addition, with the resinous, foresty note you would expect from pine oils.

brewing.notes: The traditional proportion is strong: 10 to 15 g dried or 20 to 30 g fresh needles to 60 ml water, over low heat. The time is a starting point. Add honey or sugar, and always identify the tree: not every conifer is safe.

vintage_note: No vintages. It is mostly made at home or bought as a small-batch herbal product, from needles traditionally gathered in winter. The fermented style is a fresh cold drink, ready after about a week in summer and longer in other seasons.
description:
Pine needle tea is what it sounds like: an infusion of pine needles. In Korea sollip-cha comes mostly from Korean red pine or Manchurian red pine, while jannip-cha comes from Korean pine. Japan makes matsuba-cha, mainly from red or black pine, and North Americans use local species.

There are two sollip-cha paths. In the first, needles are soaked for a day, cleaned, trimmed of their tips and cut, then infused fresh or after shade-drying. In the second, trimmed needles sit in sugar water in a sunny spot until fermented, then get filtered and served cold. Jannip-cha is simpler: fresh needles boiled, then simmered and drunk without the leaves.

The hot version is astringent, which is why honey or sugar is normal rather than a cheat. The proportions are generous, so if it is too much, dilute it.

When buying, or especially when foraging, know exactly which tree you have. Packaged needles should name the species; if a label does not, move on.

The fermented cold version is a very different drink, and worth trying if the hot one feels too medicinal.
history:
In East Asia pine needles were associated with the diet of immortals, so they were also regarded as a longevity food; that belongs to legend rather than evidence. Korean tradition carries details of its own, such as harvesting jannip-cha needles from branches growing eastward.

In North America, an often repeated account says Indigenous people taught European settlers to make the tea against scurvy, since the needles hold vitamin C.
